lessons.title: Consumer Discretionary: Retail, QSR, and Why Store Economics Matter

body.text: A retailer or restaurant chain can grow revenue 25% a year simply by opening stores, while every store it already owns sells less than last year. Growth by addition and growth by improvement look identical in the revenue line and mean completely opposite things. Same-store sales growth is how you tell them apart.

children.text: Consumer discretionary covers what Indians buy when they feel prosperous: clothes from Westside and Zudio, groceries from DMart, jewellery from Tanishq, pizza from Domino's, and burgers from McDonald's. These businesses are highly cyclical, carry heavy fixed costs in rent and staff, and are valued at some of the richest multiples in the market. Analysing them well means analysing a single store first, then multiplying.
Same-Store Sales Growth: The Number Expansion Cannot Hide

markDefs.definition: Growth in sales from stores that have been open for at least a full comparable period, usually a year. It excludes new stores, so it isolates whether existing stores are doing better or worse.

children.text: Total revenue growth for a chain comes from two sources: new stores and existing stores.

, often shortened to SSSG or called like-for-like growth, strips out new stores. It is driven by two things: how many customers transact, and how much each spends. For a restaurant chain, the equivalent measures are average daily sales per store and the split between dine-in and delivery.

body.latex: 1 + \text{SSSG} = (1 + \text{Growth in transactions}) \times (1 + \text{Growth in average bill value})
body.caption: Same-store sales growth splits into footfall or transactions and ticket size

body.title: Build Up the SSSG
body.prompt: At a fashion retailer, transactions at existing stores grew 4% over last year and the average bill value grew 3%. What is its same-store sales growth? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 1.04 × 1.03 = 1.0712, so SSSG is 7.12%. Note what each part means. Growth in transactions shows more customers or more frequent visits, which is the healthier driver. Growth in bill value can come from selling more items per visit, a richer product mix, or simply price increases, which may not last if customers resist.

body.title: Great Revenue, Shrinking Stores
body.scenario: A listed apparel chain reports 22% revenue growth for the year. In the investor presentation: it opened 80 new stores, taking the total from 340 to 420, and same-store sales growth was -3%. Gross margin is stable. Management highlights 'strong network expansion and market share gains'.
body.prompt: What is really happening, and what would decide whether this is a problem?
body.modelAnswer: All of the growth, and more, came from new stores. Existing stores sold 3% less than last year, meaning either fewer customers, smaller bills, or both. Because rent and store staff are largely fixed, negative same-store growth pressures store-level margins directly. Expansion can still be right if new stores earn good returns, but it can also hide deterioration for a few years, since every new store adds revenue regardless of quality. Decide by asking: Are new stores in new catchments, or are they cannibalising nearby existing stores? What is revenue per square foot for mature stores versus new ones, and is it falling? What is the payback period on a new store, and has it lengthened? Is negative same-store growth industry-wide, suggesting weak discretionary demand, or specific to this brand, suggesting a competitive problem? Is the company relying on discounts, which would eventually show up in gross margin? If new store returns are strong and the weakness is industry-wide, this is cyclical. If the chain is cannibalising itself while existing stores fade, the growth is borrowed from the future.

children.text: Store Economics: Analyse One Store, Then Multiply

Every retail and restaurant chain is a repeated bet on one unit. The company spends capital to fit out a store, then earns a margin on its sales. Two numbers decide whether expansion creates value: how much a mature store earns, and how long it takes to recover the money spent opening it. A chain that can open stores with a two to three year payback and keep finding good locations is a compounding machine. One with a five or six year payback is spending shareholder money on growth that may never pay off.

body.latex: \text{Store payback (years)} = \frac{\text{Capital cost per store}}{\text{Annual store-level EBITDA}} \qquad \text{Store-level EBITDA} = \text{Store revenue} \times \text{Store EBITDA margin}
body.caption: Store-level EBITDA is measured before head office costs and before any lease accounting adjustments

stats.label: Store-level EBITDA margin
stats.context: After rent, staff, and store running costs, before head office

stats.label: Capital cost per store
stats.context: Fit-out, kitchen or fixtures, and initial inventory

body.title: How Long Until the Store Pays for Itself?
body.prompt: Using the figures above, a store costs ₹2 crore to open and generates ₹72 lakh of store-level EBITDA a year once mature. Ignoring the ramp-up period, how many years does it take to recover the capital cost? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹2,00,00,000 ÷ ₹72,00,000 = 2.8 years. In reality, a new store takes time to build customer awareness, so the true payback is longer. Also note that store-level EBITDA ignores head office, marketing, and technology costs, so company-level margins are always lower than store-level margins.

body.title: Illustrative Store Maturity Curve: Revenue per Store (₹ crore a year)

body.text: The maturity curve explains a common pattern: a chain expanding very fast reports weaker average revenue per store and lower margins, because a large share of its stores are still ramping up. That is not necessarily deterioration. Ask what proportion of stores are less than two years old before judging the numbers.

body.title: Two Ways to Win in Indian Retail

columns.label: Value retail, high volume
points: Everyday low prices and thin gross margins
Profit comes from volume, inventory turns, and cost control
Owning or securing cheap real estate is a lasting advantage
Revenue per square foot is the headline efficiency measure

columns.label: Brand-led retail, high margin
points: Own brands and fashion appeal support higher gross margins
Profit depends on getting the product right and avoiding discounting
Fast product refresh cycles and store experience matter most
Watch markdowns and inventory ageing for early signs of missteps

body.title: Lease accounting: why EBITDA suddenly looks better

children.text: Under the Ind AS 116 lease accounting standard, a company records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for its stores instead of simply charging rent to the profit and loss statement. Rent no longer appears as an operating expense. Instead, the asset is depreciated and interest is charged on the lease liability. For a retailer or restaurant chain paying rent on hundreds of stores, this lifts reported EBITDA substantially without any change in the business.

content.caption: Illustrative Chain: Same Year, Two Presentations (₹ crore)

cells: Not shown as an operating cost

content.text: Never compare a post-Ind AS 116 EBITDA margin with a pre-standard historical margin, or with a peer presented differently. Most listed retailers and QSR companies disclose both. Also remember that if you use EV/EBITDA, enterprise value should include lease liabilities, or the multiple will look artificially cheap.

body.title: Which Chain Is Genuinely Doing Best?
body.question: Four restaurant chains report their year. Which shows the healthiest underlying performance?
options: Revenue +30%, store count +35%, same-store sales growth -4%, store-level margin down
Revenue +14%, store count +6%, same-store sales growth +7% driven by more transactions, store-level margin up
Revenue +18%, store count +12%, same-store sales growth +5% entirely from menu price increases, transactions down
Revenue +9%, store count +11%, same-store sales growth -2%, heavy discounting on delivery apps
body.explanation: Positive same-store growth driven by more transactions means more customers are coming, and a rising store-level margin shows operating leverage working. Option one is pure expansion masking decline. Option three grows only because of price increases while customer counts fall, which is hard to sustain. Option four combines falling same-store sales with discounting, the weakest combination.

children.text: One more force is reshaping this sector: quick commerce. Ten-minute delivery platforms have taken share in categories like groceries, snacks, and everyday essentials, pressuring both kirana stores and organised retail. For restaurants, delivery aggregators bring volume but charge commissions, so a higher delivery mix can lift sales while reducing margins. When you analyse a consumer company today, ask how much of its category is moving online and what that does to its store economics.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Growth in sales from stores open for at least a full year, excluding newly opened stores, is called ___ sales growth.
body.explanation: Same-store sales growth shows whether existing stores are improving, which total revenue growth hides when a chain is opening many new stores.

body.title: Analysing a Retail or QSR Company
steps: Separate revenue growth into new store growth and same-store sales growth
Break same-store growth into transactions and average bill value, and prefer growth led by transactions
Find store-level EBITDA margin and capital cost per store, and calculate the payback period
Check what share of the store base is less than two years old before judging average revenue per store
Check whether reported EBITDA is before or after Ind AS 116 lease accounting, and compare peers on the same basis
Track inventory levels and discounting for fashion retailers, and delivery mix and commissions for restaurant chains
Ask what the current valuation assumes about store additions and same-store growth for the next five years

points: Revenue growth for a chain mixes new stores with existing store performance; same-store sales growth separates the two
Same-store growth driven by more transactions is healthier than growth driven only by price increases
Store economics decide whether expansion creates value: mature store revenue, store-level EBITDA margin, capital cost, and payback period
New stores take years to mature, so fast expansion temporarily depresses average revenue per store and margins
Value retail wins on volume, inventory turns, and cheap real estate; brand-led retail wins on product and pricing power
Ind AS 116 lifts reported EBITDA by removing rent from operating costs, so compare like with like and include lease liabilities in enterprise value
Quick commerce and delivery aggregators are changing store economics in groceries, essentials, and restaurants
